prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: On reflection I move the optical lattice clock from third place on my opening ballot to the head of my configuration. It is exactly the kind of invention the prize exists for: a precise concept (trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels), a clean experimental demonstration, and a measured improvement of orders of magnitude in fractional frequency uncertainty. It has since been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories on several continents with Sr, Yb and other species, and clock comparisons agree at the 1e-18 level, so there is no question about whether the result is real. Its consequences are concrete: a coming redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, and searches for variation of constants. The attribution is also unusually clean. Katori made the proposal and the first lattice clock; Ye's group took the approach to record accuracy and stability and to many-body clock physics. Two names map onto two distinct, decisive contributions. This is a discovery or invention with an identifiable origin and identifiable people, and it is a topic where five of the eight members rank it in their top six, three of them first.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to recent recognition: the 2005 prize (Hall and Hänsch) covered the frequency comb that makes optical clocks countable, and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) covered control of single quantum systems and ion clocks, so a skeptic can say that the optical-clock lineage has been honoured twice. Second, the SI redefinition is still pending and some colleagues would wait for it. Third, a two-name prize leaves out other Sr and Yb lattice groups and the Paris and PTB teams, and I cannot verify from the files alone how decisive their early contributions were. Finally, an atomic-physics or precision-measurement prize in 2026 follows the 2025 circuit-physics award in the broader quantum-technology area, and the committee should not simply rotate toward the same community. I weigh these as real but not decisive: the lattice clock is a distinct invention, not an application of earlier prizes.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as the clearest case where laser spectroscopy changed what can be measured, with a clean two-name configuration (Katori the magic-wavelength proposal, Ye the systematic-uncertainty and stability record) and high maturity across many independent labs.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this and it is the main reason I have moved it up. Where I differ from Kroll is on how firmly the two-name configuration can be defended. He suggests not widening it, but he also lists Lemonde, Takamoto and others as possible additions, and that is a live attribution question rather than a footnote. I would keep Katori and Ye because the proposal and the record-setting realisation are separable and decisive, while the contributions of other groups refine the method. I would want the citation to name the invention (magic-wavelength lattice clocks) so that it does not read as a general prize for optical clocks.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clock first but asks whether recognition should be held until the redefinition of the second is settled, and whether Ye's role is a realisation rather than a co-invention.
responses.response: I do not think the prize should wait for the SI redefinition. The criterion is a discovery or invention with demonstrated impact, and the clock's accuracy and its comparisons between laboratories already establish that; the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows from the achievement, not a test of it. On Ye's role I partly concede her point: the original concept is Katori's. But Ye's group did not merely realise it; it drove the accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics that made the clock a new instrument, and I regard that as a separate scientific contribution, so a two-person prize is justified. I would want the committee to be explicit that the citation reflects both.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the topological insulators (B038) first as a conceptually deep, over fifteen-year-confirmed field that is arguably overdue, with Kane and Mele for theory and Molenkamp for the HgTe experiment.
responses.response: I accept the field's importance, and I ranked it sixth rather than lower. My difficulty is the attribution and overlap, not the physics. The Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal that actually led to the HgTe experiment is outside the credited names, Zhang has died, and the 3D materials work is also outside; a prize for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would therefore have a visible gap in the middle of the story. The 2016 prize on topological phases also covers the broader territory, which Mehlig himself notes. I would revisit this if colleagues can show a citation that is clearly limited to the Z2 prediction and the QSH observation, but I do not think it is the strongest candidate this year.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture of virtually all leading superconducting processors, noting that the credit among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff is partly contested and cannot be cut to three without excluding a major contributor.
responses.response: I ranked circuit QED second and regard it as an excellent candidate, and Johansson's own admission that the three-name limit excludes a decisive contributor is the key difficulty for me; Lindroth and Kroll both add that a closely related award follows soon after the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits. Where I disagree is on weighing the technological impact: platform dominance is evidence of impact, but the committee should credit the original idea and demonstration rather than the engineering that followed. I therefore keep it as an alternative, and I would like to hear whether there is a defensible citation that avoids splitting Girvin from Blais.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the clock first too, but places twisted bilayer graphene seventh because it is relatively young, the pairing mechanism is unsettled, and Cao and earlier theorists are not credited.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me. My own opening ballot put twisted bilayer graphene first on the strength of a precise, falsifiable prediction followed by experiment, but Pearce and several others rank it low mainly on maturity and the unresolved superconducting mechanism, and Eriksson is the only member who ranks it first alongside me. I still believe the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated insulators are secure and that a prize would not need to rest on the pairing mechanism, so I keep B042 as an alternative. However, when the ranking is spread this widely, I am not confident a prize this year would command committee agreement, and I would not put the less settled field ahead of the clock.

uncertainties: Whether Hall, Hänsch, Wineland and the optical-clock lineage reduce novelty enough to count against the lattice clock, and whether other Sr and Yb groups need to be credited.
How much of the experimental credit between Katori and Ye is separable, given that I am relying on recollection of the achieved uncertainties rather than verified figures.

Whether the committee prefers to wait for twisted bilayer graphene to mature, since a decision depends on how the superconducting pairing question is resolved and on credit for Cao and early continuum-model authors.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the optical lattice clock candidate or its credited names. My documented connections are to microscopy and materials physics, to David R. Clarke, to Japanese academic exchanges, and to Chalmers colleagues; Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers, which is a general institutional link but not a candidate-specific tie. I have documented Japanese academic exchanges, and Katori is at a Japanese institution; I know of no personal connection to him, but I flag the general link for transparency.
